newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian firms see China business as usual.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian firms see China business as usual.

text.p: Australian companies with interests in China said on Thursday the death of Deng Xiaoping was unlikely to affect existing or planned investment.

Tim Meakin, chief executive officer of pharmaceutical manufacturer F.H. Faulding & Co Ltd's Chinese operating arm, said he expected no dramatic changes in policy towards western investment. "I think there will be business as usual. I hope I'm not proven wrong," he told Reuters.

Meakin said Faulding, like other pharmaceutical ventures, had struggled in China over the last six months due to the impact of Beijing's austerity programme. "The last six months in China have been fairly tough," he said. "We would hope that the future will be a little less restrictive."
Meakin said Faulding had invested A$35 million since November 1994 in its Chinese manufacturing facilties for oral generic products and importation and distribution operations.
Paper and packaging group Amcor ltd said operations at its four plants in China would continue unchanged.
"It's business as usual as far as we're concerned," said general manager of corporate affairs, Peter Cairns.

Amcor, which earned about three percent of its gross sales from the Asian region in 1995/96 (July-June), is about to finish construction of its fifth Chinese facility, a cigarette packaging plant, in Kunming.
Banking and insurance group Colonial Mutual, which has two representative offices in China and has applied for a licence to operate throughout the country, also saw little change.

"We just see the processes continuing in the ordinary way that they have done for some time and we would expect from a commercial point of view that process to continue," said the group's Asia/Pacific general manager, Alan Beanland.

Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd, which has a strong Asia/Pacific presence, said it was too early to properly assess the impact of Deng's death but it remained hopeful of success in its push for a second banking licence in China. "We certainly continue to be hopeful our application will be viewed favourably," said spokesman David Wilson.
"We take the Chinese market very seriously," Wilson said.
"It's a place of burgeoning trade and investment growth and we are very keen to strengthen our presence," he added.
Industrial products manufacturer Pacific BBA Ltd also expected its involvement with China to continue unfettered by a change in the Chinese leadership.
"(Deng) was an elderly man and his condition has been well known for some time, so we don't expect there to be any sudden changes there," said managing director Barry Jackson.
But he said the firm was taking a cautious approach with plans to build a A$10 million construction products plant there.
"We'll obviously be monitoring the situation in China before making a decision," Jackson told Reuters.
Australia's prime minister John Howard earlier forecast ties with China would remain stable.
"I don't expect it will make a fundamental change to either relations between Australia and China," he said.
